question: Regardless of recycling method, there will always be a share of waste that cannot be recycled. The emissions from non-recyclable waste are unavoidable and the best way to treat them is by incineration combined with energy recovery. The Carbon Removal Certification Framework provides an incentive for the capture, utilisation, and storage of biogenic emissions from waste incineration.

However, there are currently no incentives to reduce fossil-emissions from waste incineration or the incineration of hazardous waste. Even if waste incineration plants are included in EU-ETS, the gap between the cost of carbon capture and storage (CCS) solutions and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS) price is significant and indications about the future ETS prices lacking.
This price imbalance incentivises the incineration of biogenic waste, which could be recycled in line with the waste hierarchy. 1.
In addition to carbon pricing, what other policy measures is the Commission considering to promote carbon capture in the waste-to-energy (WtE) sector?
What kind of role does the Commission envision for CCU in the WtE sector considering that the unavoidable emissions from incinerating non-recyclable waste include fossil-based material?
The inclusion of municipal waste incineration in the ETS favours the incineration of biogenic waste fractions over better recycling. How will the Commission address this problem?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.5.

2024) The Communication ‘Towards an ambitious Industrial Carbon Management for the EU’1 recalls that the 2026 review of the EU emissions trading system (ETS)2 will assess the feasibility of including municipal waste incineration installations and other waste management processes, notably landfilling, in the EU ETS, taking into account relevant criteria such as environmental integrity and alignment with the objectives of the circular economy and the Waste Framework Directive3.

In addition, under the provisional agreement on the carbon removals certification framework4, the captured biogenic emissions from waste to energy plants could benefit from the certification of carbon removals whenever the quality and sustainability criteria, as well as all the other conditions set by the Regulation are met.

Among the announced actions in the above-mentioned Communication there is a list of actions to incentivise and de-risk investments in carbon capture and utilisation and carbon capture and storage (CCU/CCS) technologies, including further push of research and innovation to yield significant cost reduction and to initiate work for a possible future CO2 transport regulatory package to facilitate access to storage.

Under the waste hierarchy, the priority is prevention, followed by preparing for re-use, recycling, other recovery, e.g. energy recovery, and disposal only as a last resort5. In this context, the Commission has for example proposed a Regulation to ensure that all packaging is recyclable in an economically viable way by 20306.
CCU/CCS could reduce emissions from incineration of truly unavoidable and non-recyclable waste.
